opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core tension with on-policy RL is that your data distribution is a moving target, and you're the one moving it. In supervised learning you have a fixed dataset; you can shuffle it, iterate on it, and your loss curves mean something stable. When samples come from your own policy, every gradient step changes the distribution you'll see next. So you get this feedback loop: if the policy drifts into some weird corner of state space, now all your training data comes from that weird corner, and it can reinforce itself. Things collapse in ways that are really hard to diagnose, because you can't easily tell whether the problem is the optimizer, the reward, or just that the data has quietly shifted under you.

The second thing is exploration. The policy can only learn from what it actually tries. If the good behavior is rare under the current policy, you basically never see it, and you never get the signal to move toward it. That's partly why pretraining matters so much for something like an LLM. A strong prior means the on-policy samples are already in a reasonable neighborhood, so RL is sharpening rather than searching from scratch. In robotics you often don't have that luxury. A randomly initialized or weakly pretrained policy flails around, and most of the samples are uninformative.

Third is sample cost. On-policy means you throw data away after you update, or at least it goes stale fast. In simulation or with text, generating more rollouts is cheap-ish. On a real robot, every rollout is wall-clock time, wear on hardware, someone resetting the scene. So the data efficiency gap between on-policy methods and what you'd want is enormous.

And then there's variance. The gradient estimates are noisy because you're estimating returns from a handful of trajectories with high-variance outcomes. You end up spending a lot of engineering effort on baselines, clipping, KL penalties, normalization, all these tricks that are really about keeping the policy from taking a step that ruins its own future data.

So the way I'd summarize it is that on-policy RL couples learning and data collection, and that coupling is both why it works, since you get feedback on exactly what you do, and why it's so fragile.

r001.rationale: The response says the policy can only learn from what it tries, so an outcome it has zero probability of sampling provides no learning signal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that makes on-policy RL hard, in my experience, is that you're basically building a learning system that has to teach itself from its own mistakes, and the quality of what it learns is bounded by what it's already willing to try. If the policy never samples the right behavior, there's no gradient signal pointing you toward it. You can't learn from what you never see. So early on, when the model is bad, you're sampling a lot of garbage, and the reward is almost always zero or near zero, and you're just sitting there waiting for a lucky rollout. People call this the exploration problem, but I think that undersells how brutal it is in practice. It's really a chicken-and-egg problem: you need a decent policy to get useful samples, and you need useful samples to get a decent policy.

The second thing is that the data distribution is non-stationary. Every time you update the policy, the distribution of states and actions you're going to see next changes. In supervised learning you have this fixed dataset, you can tune your hyperparameters, you can reason about overfitting, the loss curve means something. In on-policy RL, the loss curve means almost nothing, because the thing you're computing the loss on keeps moving under you. You can have the loss go down and the policy get worse. You can have a bug that silently makes everything slightly off-policy and the whole thing just quietly degrades without ever throwing an error. Debugging is miserable because there's no ground truth to compare against. You're always asking, is this the algorithm, is this the reward, is this the sampler, is this a distribution shift I introduced three updates ago?

And then there's the sample efficiency problem, which is really a cost problem. Because you can't reuse data very well, you throw away most of what you collect after one or a few gradient steps. For a language model or a robot policy, generating those samples is expensive. In robotics it's physically expensive, the robot has to actually do things, you can only run so many episodes a day. With LLMs you can parallelize, but you're still spending a huge amount of compute on inference just to produce training data, and most of that data is low-information. So you end up with this very expensive flywheel where the thing that's hardest to get is the exact thing you need the most.

The last piece, and the one I think about a lot, is that the model will exploit whatever reward you give it, and because it's sampling from its own distribution, it's actively searching for the holes in your reward function. Supervised learning doesn't do that. A dataset doesn't fight back. An RL policy does. So you spend a lot of your time not on the algorithm at all but on reward design, on building verifiers, on figuring out how to make it hard to cheat. And you're never sure you've closed every hole until the policy finds the next one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that if the policy never samples the right behavior, there is no gradient signal pointing toward it, and that it cannot learn from what it never sees.

astra-6.text:
The tricky thing is that the model determines what data it gets to learn from. In supervised learning, you can hold the dataset fixed and ask whether your optimization is working. In reinforcement learning, every update changes the policy, which changes the distribution of experiences you collect next.

So you can get these feedback loops. If the model becomes slightly less likely to try something, it collects less evidence about whether that thing is useful, and it can become even less likely to try it. A behavior might be valuable, but if your policy almost never samples it, you don’t get the learning signal that would make it more probable.

That makes exploration and optimization really entangled. When learning stalls, is it because the model can’t represent the right behavior, because the update isn’t working, or because it simply never encountered the experiences it needed? Those are difficult to tease apart when your learner is also generating its own training data.

r001.rationale: The response says that a behavior the policy “almost never” samples lacks a learning signal, but it does not state the specific case where the policy assigns it zero probability.

sol-6.1.text:
The tricky thing is that the model determines what data it gets to learn from. If your policy never tries something, you never find out whether it was good. So you can get stuck in this feedback loop where you sample the things you already think are likely, reinforce whichever ones happen to work, and never discover a much better strategy outside that distribution.

And the distribution keeps changing as you learn. You’re updating the policy, which changes the experiences you collect, which changes your next update. So unlike supervised learning, where you can hold the dataset fixed and debug the optimization, here exploration, data collection, and optimization are all coupled. When something isn’t learning, it can be hard to tell whether the model can’t represent the solution, the optimizer can’t find it, or you simply never sampled the experience that would teach it.

r001.rationale: It says that if the policy never tries an action, it never learns whether it was good, capturing the lack of learning signal for an outcome the policy cannot sample.
